newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to review, modify African defence accords.
newsitem.headline: France to review, modify African defence accords.

text.p: Cooperation Minister Charles Josselin said on Thursday France's new Socialist administration would review defence accords with former African colonies, indicating Paris wanted some disengagement from the area.
"I can confirm the dossier is open and the defence accords with African states will be updated," Josselin told a news conference.

"Today's Africa is not what it was in the 1960s, the French army is itself being reorganised and the notion of mobility has changed," said Josselin, adding that defence cooperation would be redefined.
"There is also a will on the part of the African states, which we encourage, to themselves take over security roles, even in a regional capacity," Josselin said.
He said the future missions of the French army in Africa would be aimed mostly at ensuring "security rather than defence and preparing for peace".

France has intervened dozens of times across Africa since granting its former colonies independence in the early 1960s, mostly to prop up governments friendly to Paris but also in Zaire and Rwanda which were Belgian rather than French possessions.
The French Socialist party has long been critical of the country's African policy which it said perpetuated neo-colonial relations and backed dictators.
But Socialist President Francois Mitterrand carried out virtually the same policies as his centre-right predecessors when he was in power from 1981 to 1995.

Paris' African policy has been in tatters in the last two years with the fall of regimes friendly to France in Zaire and Rwanda and open civil strife breaking out in countries like the Congo and the Central African Republic.
France has formal defence accords with Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Comoros, Ivory Coast, Djibouti, Gabon, Senegal and Togo.
Between 8,000 and 10,000 French troops are permanently based in some of those countries whose current leaders have mostly asked Paris not to close garrisons there.

Recurrent reports in Paris newspapers say French leaders, including the Socialists, believe the United States wishes to replace France as the virtual "protecting power" in the region whose raw materials represent wide economic potential.

Josselin himself made an oblique reference to this when he said "certain countries" sought to draw African elites towards themselves by citing France's tight immigration laws which are resented in French-speaking African states.
Josselin also said he believed the situation in central Africa was critical and he warned that the current internecine fighting in the Congo might serve as an example for neighbouring states.
